div.head: Background
div.p: In the Eplerenone in Mild Patients Hospitalization and Survival Study in Heart Failure (EMPHASIS-HF) trial, the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) eplerenone was shown to reduce cardiovascular death or hospitalizations for heart failure (HF) in patients with systolic HF and mild symptoms. 1 Although a consistent body of evidence supports the conclusion that MRAs significa nt l y improve clinical outcomes, these drugs remain underused. 2 In particular some characteristics -such as lower creatinine clearance, older age, outpatient setting, and ischaemic heart disease -are more frequently associated with MRA underutilization in clinical practice. 3 In addition, clinical inertia and therapeutic hesitancy, especially in a population mistakenly thought to be clinically stable and/or with relatively mild symptoms -such as that studied in the EMPHASIS-HF -may delay the implementation of effective therapies. Understanding the timing of benefit, particularly in those subgroups where MRAs are under-used, may help clinicians to better understand the treatment effect and consequently optimise the prescription of these drugs. Herein, we conducted a post hoc analys is of the EMPHASIS-HF trial to investigate the treatment effect of eplerenone over time in patients with HFrEF and in key subgroups.

div.head: Methods
div.p: The EMPHASIS-HF trial was a multicentre, double-blinded, randomized clinical trial to assess the effects of eplerenone in patients with chronic systolic HF and mild symptoms. The protocol and the outcomes of the EMPHASIS-HF trial have been previously described. 1 Key inclusion criteria were: age ≥ 55 years, New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class II symptoms, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤30% (or LVEF 30% -35% and QRS duration >130 msec), 6 months from the last cardiovascular hospitalization or high natriuretic peptides. The primary outcome was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes or a first hospitalization for HF.

Hazard ratios (HR) were calculated on each day following randomization until the last observation of the last patient using the Cox proportional hazards model. The MAGGIC score was calculated as previously described. 4 The study protocol was approved by local ethics committees or institutional review boards at each participating site, and each patient provided written informed consent. Statistical analyses were performed using R software (the R Foundation for Statistical Computing) version 4.1.2. Two-sided P values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

div.head: Results
div.p: 18790844, ja, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ejhf.2952 by <Shibboleth>-member@gla.ac.uk, Wiley Online Library on [03/07/2023]. See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License Baseline characteristics of the studied population are reported in Table 1. A total of 2737 patients at 278 centers in 29 countries were randomly assigned to placebo (n=1373) or to eplerenone (n=1364).

The mean ± SD age was 68.6 ± 7.6 years (67.7% ≥ 65 years, 24% ≥ 75 years), 610 (22.3%) were women and in 1886 (68.9%) the HF aetiology was ischemic. The median [percentile25-75] duration of HF was 2.4 [0.4 -7.0] years and 1438 (52.6%) patients experienced a previous hospitalization for HF. The mean MAGGIC score was 22.0 ± 4.8. A total of 2651 patients (97.5%) was treated with a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor and 2374 (87.2%) with a betablocker. No significant differences were found in baseline characteristics between eplerenone arm and placebo arm.

Among the 2737 patients randomized, 605 primary end point events occurred over a median follow-up of 21 months. At the end of follow-up, eplerenone significantly reduced the primary end point by 34% (HR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.56-0.78; P < 0.001) (Figure 1A). Time to first nominal statistica l significance for the primary end point was 26 days (HR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.34-1.00; P = 0.049), and was largely sustained during follow-up (i.e. from day 26 to the end of the trial the confidence interva l remained below unity) (Figure 1B; Table 2). Eplerenone was first associated with a significa nt reduction in the primary endpoint in 35 days or less in most subgroups, including patients with HF history ≥ 18 months (day 24; HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.22-0.97), eGFR < 60 ml/min (day 12; HR, 0.12; 95% CI, 0.02-0.97), LVEF ≥ 30% (day 28; HR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.13-0.99), ischemic HF aetiology (day 28; HR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.28-0.98), age ≥ 65 (day 28; HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.23-0.92), higher MAGGIC score (day 35; HR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.29-0.93), narrow QRS (day 30; HR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.27-0.96), lower potassium (day 30; HR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.26-1.00), or already treated with betablockers (day 25; HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.31-1.00) (Figure 2). The timing of sustained statistica l significance mostly coincided with the time to first nominal clinical benefit, except for eGFR (day 26), LVEF (day 65), MAGGIC score (day 42) and serum potassium (day 35) (Table 2).

Analysis by age strata showed that eplerenone treatment led to a similar early reduction in the primary endpoint in patients ≥ 70 years (day 39; HR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.23-0.96) and ≥ 75 years (day 40; HR, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.14-0.93). div.head: Discussion
div.p: In this analysis we present evidence that eplerenone induces an early (<35 days) and sustained significant reduction in clinical events in patients with HFrEF and mild symptoms. This result is important for the therapeutic approach to patients with HFrEF, especially in the context of the current debate of guideline-directed medical therapy sequencing. 5 Our findings are highly consistent with similar observations from a recent pooled HFrEF cohort showing that treatment with MRAs induced a significant statistical reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by day 19 of randomization. 6 Notably, the results we present herein demonstrate that most subgroups, by definition smaller than the whole cohort, had an early and sustained benefit from eplerenone treatment. This finding has relevant practical implications since in the Swedish HF Registry some of these clinical profilesnamely lower renal function (< 60 mL/min), higher LVEF, older age, and ischaemic heart diseaseshowed a lower probability of receiving MRAs. 3 Of particular interest, chronic kidney disease was demonstrated the stronger predictor of MRA non-use, even in the creatinine clearance 30 -60 mL/min range. 3 In this regard, we showed that a sustained reduction in clinical events was achieved by day 26 from randomization in patients with eGFR < 60 mL/min, but only by day 77 in patients with eGFR > 60 mL/min. The same pattern was observed for those with ischemic heart disease. In older patients MRAs are frequently underused due to concern for side-effects, although the clinical benefit seems to be consistent also in this subgroup. 7 We showed that eplerenone treatment induced an early and sustained benefit in patients ≥ 65 years, ≥ 70 years or ≥ 75 years. Of note, the sustained statistica l significance is obtained earlier in patients ≥ 65 years vs. < 65 or ≥ 70 years vs. <70. We also demonstrated that patients already treated with betablockers had the earliest clinica l benefit. This is in line with the acquisition that HF drugs act synergistically, with the larger estimated benefit using a combination of the four pillars of HF foundational therapy. 8 Finally, it should be acknowledged that our findings are derived from a HF cohort usually perceived at low risk of clinica l events (mild symptoms), though it is not (i.e. in EMPHASIS-HF the incidence of the composite endpoint in the placebo arm was 26%). 1 Our study has a few limitations to consider, namely those inherent to post hoc analyses. The time-to-first statistical significance is strongly influenced by relative number of accrued events. Accordingly, we decided to restrict our analysis only to the primary composite endpoint (that had the larger number of events). Our approach, as all similar studies in the field of HF, primarily focused on the time to first statistical significance. This strategy is exposed to the issue of multiple testing. In addition, sample size has an important impact on p-value. However, other approaches, i.e. targeting to solve an equation for time to effect, are not readily available. In addition, our analysis highlight, using the same approach that has been used in other trials for other pharmacological class, 9, 10 that overall MRAs acts fast regardless of the considered sub-groups. The EMPHASIS-HF trial was conducted before the introduction of sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors and sacubitril/valsartan. Therefore, our results should be interpreted in context of the current background therapy. However, most reports show that the effect of HF treatments are actually independent from one another, as highlighted by the absence of significant statistical interaction identified in post-hoc analysis of trials. [11][12][13] In conclusion, this post hoc analysis demonstrates that treatment with eplerenone provides clinically and statistically significant benefits shortly after treatment initiation (in most instances <35 days), which are sustained long term, both in the overall population and in specific subgroups. Therefore, our findings may help physicians to recognize the therapeutic potential of eplerenone, mainly in that clinical subgroups where MRAs are more frequently underused.
